course.title: AP Precalculus
course.description: Build the function toolkit that calculus depends on: how quantities change together, polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic models, and trigonometric and polar functions.
course.previewDescription: Study how outputs change with inputs, then use polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions to describe patterns and build models.

unit.title: Polynomial and Rational Functions

topic.title: Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation
topic.summary: Choosing a linear, quadratic, polynomial, or piecewise-defined model from a data set or context, and stating the assumptions and domain and range restrictions of a model.

lesson.title: Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation
lesson.summary: Choosing a linear, quadratic, polynomial, or piecewise-defined model from a data set or context, and stating the assumptions and domain and range restrictions of a model.
learningGoals: 1.13.A Identify an appropriate function type to construct a function model for a given scenario.
1.13.B Describe assumptions and restrictions related to building a function model.
lesson.bigIdea: A function model is chosen by matching how the quantities in a data set or context change to how a function type changes. Every model also carries assumptions about what stays consistent, and restrictions on its domain and range.
lesson.context: You now know how linear, quadratic, and other polynomial functions change. This topic asks which type to choose and how to justify the choice, a part that appears in free-response Question 1 and Question 2 of the AP Exam.

sections.title: 1.13.A · The pattern of change in a data set or context points to a function type.

blocks.caption: Matching scenarios to function types
columns: The data set or context shows
rows: Roughly linear rates of change, or roughly symmetric data with a unique maximum or minimum
A geometric context involving area or two dimensions
A geometric context involving volume or three dimensions
Multiple real zeros, or multiple maxima or minima
Roughly constant nonzero nth differences over equal-length input-value intervals

blocks.text: An open box made by cutting squares of side x from the corners of a sheet has volume x(30 − 2x)(20 − 2x), a cubic function of x, because volume involves three dimensions. The area of a rectangle with a fixed perimeter is a quadratic function of its width, because area involves two dimensions.

sections.takeaway: Describe how the output values change, then choose the function type that changes the same way.

sections.title: 1.13.A · A polynomial of degree n models roughly constant nonzero nth differences.

blocks.text: A polynomial function of degree n models data sets or contextual scenarios that demonstrate roughly constant nonzero nth differences. Also, a polynomial function of degree n or less can be used to model a graph of n + 1 points with distinct input values, so 3 points can always be fit by a quadratic function or a line.

blocks.caption: Successive differences for data at x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

blocks.title: Write it like the AP Exam
blocks.text: Because the 3rd differences in the output values are a constant 6 over consecutive equal-length input-value intervals, a cubic model is best. Refer to the values from the table in the reason.

sections.takeaway: Name the constant difference, the level at which it appears, and the equal-length intervals.

sections.title: 1.13.A · A piecewise-defined function models different behavior on different intervals.

blocks.text: A piecewise-defined function consists of a set of functions defined over nonoverlapping domain intervals. It is useful for modeling a data set or contextual scenario that demonstrates different characteristics over different intervals.

A parking garage charges $3 per hour for the first 2 hours and $1 per hour after that. The cost is modeled by C(t) = 3t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 and C(t) = 6 + (t − 2) for t > 2. Each piece is linear, but the rate of change is 3 dollars per hour on the first interval and 1 dollar per hour on the second.

blocks.caption: Parking cost C(t): two linear pieces that meet at t = 2
blocks.alt: A line from (0, 0) to (2, 6) with slope 3, followed by a less steep line from (2, 6) with slope 1.

sections.takeaway: Use a piecewise-defined model when the rate or pattern changes at a known input value.

sections.title: 1.13.B · Models have assumptions and domain and range restrictions.

items: A model may assume something is consistent, such as a constant growth rate or a fixed price.
A model may assume how the quantities change together, such as a constant rate of change for a linear model.
A model may require domain restrictions based on mathematical clues, contextual clues, or extreme values in the data set.
A model may require range restrictions, such as rounding to whole numbers, based on mathematical clues, contextual clues, or extreme values in the data set.

blocks.text: A ball thrown from a height of 5 feet has height h(t) = −16t² + 48t + 5 feet after t seconds. The model assumes only gravity acts on the ball. Its domain is restricted to 0 ≤ t ≤ 3.101, from the throw until the ball lands, and its range to 0 ≤ h(t) ≤ 41, since the maximum height is h(1.5) = 41.

blocks.title: Write it like the AP Exam
blocks.text: The model is appropriate until the ball lands, when h(t) = 0 at t = 3.101 seconds. The throw is at t = 0. Therefore, an appropriate domain for the model h is [0, 3.101] seconds.

sections.takeaway: State the assumption, the domain, and the range in the language of the context.

vocabulary.definition: A piecewise-defined function consists of a set of functions defined over nonoverlapping domain intervals and is useful for modeling a data set or contextual scenario that demonstrates different characteristics over different intervals.
A model may have underlying assumptions about what is consistent in the model. A model may have underlying assumptions about how quantities change together.

connections.title: Rates of change were the evidence
connections.body: Topic 1.3 showed that linear functions have constant average rates of change and quadratic functions have average rates of change that change at a constant rate. Successive differences apply that idea to a data table.
connections.transferQuestion: Why does a constant 2nd difference point to a quadratic model?
connections.feedback: The 1st differences, which are average rates of change over equal-length intervals, change at a constant rate.

connections.title: From choosing to constructing
connections.body: Topic 1.14 finds the constants of the chosen model from conditions, transformations, or regression, and then uses the model to answer questions.
connections.transferQuestion: Once you choose a quadratic model, what do you need to find its equation?
connections.feedback: Three conditions, such as three points, or a vertex and one more point.

glossary.definition: The set of input values is called the domain of the function, and the set of output values is called the range of the function.
The set of input values is called the domain of the function, and the set of output values is called the range of the function.

The average rate of change of a function over an interval of the function’s domain is the constant rate of change that yields the same change in the output values as the function yielded on that interval of the function’s domain. It is the ratio of the change in the output values to the change in input values over that interval.
For a quadratic function, the average rates of change over consecutive equal-length input-value intervals can be given by a linear function.

The degree of a polynomial function can be found by examining the successive differences of the output values over equal-interval input values. The degree of the polynomial function is equal to the least value n for which the successive nth differences are constant.

A piecewise-defined function consists of a set of functions defined over nonoverlapping domain intervals and is useful for modeling a data set or contextual scenario that demonstrates different characteristics over different intervals.
A model may have underlying assumptions about what is consistent in the model. A model may have underlying assumptions about how quantities change together.
